electrochem-eng-001.question: Which correctly gives the meaning and value of the Faraday constant F used in electrolysis calculations?
choices: The charge carried by one electron, about 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C
The magnitude of the charge carried by 1 mol of electrons, about 9.65×10⁴ C/mol
The charge passed when a current of 1 A flows for 1 hour, 3600 C
electrochem-eng-001.explanation: The Faraday constant is the magnitude of the charge per mole of electrons: the product of the elementary charge e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C and the Avogadro constant 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹, giving F ≈ 96485 C/mol (about 9.65×10⁴ C/mol). By Faraday's law, the amount of substance reacting at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, Q = It, and for a z-electron reaction n = Q/(zF) [mol]. The charge of one electron is the elementary charge itself and cannot be used directly in calculations in moles. 3600 C is the charge of 1 A·h, which is used to express battery capacity, but it is a different quantity from F (F corresponds to about 26.8 A·h/mol).

electrochem-eng-002.question: In the electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate, copper is deposited at the cathode by Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. If a current of 10 A flows for 1 hour with a current efficiency of 100%, about how many grams of copper are deposited? Take the molar mass of Cu as 63.55 g/mol and F = 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 11.9 g
About 23.7 g
About 0.20 g
electrochem-eng-002.explanation: The charge passed is Q = It = 10 × 3600 = 3.6×10⁴ C. Depositing 1 mol of copper requires 2 mol of electrons, so the amount deposited is n = Q/(2F) = 3.6×10⁴ ÷ (2 × 96485) ≈ 0.187 mol, and the mass is 0.187 × 63.55 ≈ 11.9 g. About 23.7 g is the value obtained by forgetting that z = 2 and taking z = 1, and about 0.20 g corresponds to mistaking 1 hour for 60 s. In real electrolysis part of the current goes to side reactions such as hydrogen evolution, so the amount deposited is lower by the current efficiency.

electrochem-eng-003.question: In electrowinning of a metal, which is the main reason the current efficiency falls below 100%?
choices: The electrolyte resistance is high, so ohmic loss raises the cell voltage and that portion of the current is lost as heat
The electrode overpotentials are large, so the cell voltage exceeds the theoretical decomposition voltage and part of the charge goes unused by any reaction
Part of the current passed is used for side reactions such as hydrogen evolution at the cathode, or for redissolution of the deposit
electrochem-eng-003.explanation: Current efficiency is the charge used for the desired reaction divided by the total charge passed, and it is measured as the ratio of the actual amount produced to the theoretical amount from Faraday's law. It is lowered by side reactions such as hydrogen evolution at the cathode, back reactions or redissolution of the product at the counter electrode or in the electrolyte, leakage currents and so on, in which charge is not converted into the desired product. Ohmic loss and overpotential push up the cell voltage and worsen the voltage efficiency (energy consumed), but they do not change how the charge itself is used, so they are losses separate from current efficiency. Specific energy consumption depends on both of these efficiencies.

electrochem-eng-004.question: Which correctly describes how the components of an electrolytic cell's voltage depend on current density?
choices: The theoretical decomposition voltage is nearly constant regardless of current density, while the overpotentials and ohmic loss increase as current density increases
The theoretical decomposition voltage increases in proportion to current density, while the overpotentials are constant regardless of current density
The ohmic loss is constant regardless of current density, and only the overpotentials increase with current density
electrochem-eng-004.explanation: The cell voltage is broken down as V = E (theoretical decomposition voltage) + ηa (anode overpotential) + |ηc| (cathode overpotential) + IR (ohmic loss in the electrolyte, separator, electrodes and conductors). The theoretical decomposition voltage is a thermodynamic value set by the Gibbs energy change of the reaction through E = ΔG/(zF); it changes with temperature and concentration but does not depend on current. The overpotential is the extra voltage needed to drive the reaction at a finite rate, and it increases with current density, as in the Tafel equation η = a + b·log i. The ohmic loss is proportional to current. Making the theoretical decomposition voltage proportional to current, or treating the ohmic loss as constant, is wrong.

electrochem-eng-005.question: A water electrolyzer is operated at a current density of 4000 A/m². With a theoretical decomposition voltage of 1.23 V, an anode overpotential of 0.30 V, a cathode overpotential of 0.20 V, an electrode gap of 3.0 mm and an assumed electrolyte conductivity of 50 S/m (an effective value including the effect of bubbles), what is the approximate cell voltage (ignore the resistance of the separator and conductors)?
choices: About 1.73 V
About 1.97 V
About 2.22 V
electrochem-eng-005.explanation: The ohmic loss in the electrolyte is current density × electrode gap ÷ conductivity = 4000 × 0.0030 ÷ 50 = 0.24 V. Adding the theoretical decomposition voltage and the overpotentials at both electrodes gives a cell voltage of 1.23 + 0.30 + 0.20 + 0.24 = 1.97 V. About 1.73 V leaves out the ohmic loss, and about 2.22 V uses the thermoneutral voltage of 1.48 V instead of the theoretical decomposition voltage. The conductivity of 50 S/m is an assumption for the calculation; the real value depends on concentration, temperature and the amount of gas bubbles. Ohmic loss is reduced by narrowing the gap (zero-gap designs), operating at concentrations and temperatures with high conductivity, and letting bubbles escape to the back of the electrodes.

electrochem-eng-006.question: Water electrolysis is used to produce 1 Nm³ of hydrogen (44.6 mol, taking 22.4 L/mol at 0 ℃ and 101.325 kPa). With a cell voltage of 2.0 V and a current efficiency of 100%, about how much electrical energy (specific energy consumption) is required? Take F = 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 2.4 kWh/Nm³
About 2.9 kWh/Nm³
About 4.8 kWh/Nm³
electrochem-eng-006.explanation: Hydrogen is formed by 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (in alkaline media 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻), so each mole requires 2 mol of electrons. The charge needed is Q = 2 × 44.6 × 96485 ≈ 8.61×10⁶ C, and the energy is W = QV = 8.61×10⁶ × 2.0 ≈ 1.72×10⁷ J; dividing by 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J gives about 4.8 kWh/Nm³. About 2.4 kWh/Nm³ takes the number of electrons as 1, and about 2.9 kWh/Nm³ uses the theoretical decomposition voltage of 1.23 V instead of the cell voltage, which corresponds to the thermodynamic lower limit. Specific energy consumption is roughly proportional to cell voltage, so reducing overpotential and ohmic loss is the key to saving power.

electrochem-eng-007.question: Which correctly describes chlor-alkali electrolysis by the ion-exchange membrane process?
choices: Saturated brine is fed to the anode compartment, where chlorine is evolved; Na⁺ passes through a cation-exchange membrane into the cathode compartment, where sodium hydroxide and hydrogen are formed
Saturated brine is fed to the cathode compartment, Cl⁻ passes through an anion-exchange membrane into the anode compartment, and sodium hydroxide is formed in the anode compartment
Hydrogen is evolved at the anode and chlorine at the cathode, and the membrane only prevents the gases from mixing, passing neither ions nor current
electrochem-eng-007.explanation: At the anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ takes place, and at the cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. The fluorinated cation-exchange membrane between the two compartments selectively passes Na⁺ and hardly passes Cl⁻ or OH⁻, so the Na⁺ that has moved from the anode compartment and the OH⁻ produced at the cathode form sodium hydroxide in the cathode compartment. Saying an anion-exchange membrane is used and NaOH forms in the anode compartment gets both the membrane type and the direction of ion movement backwards. Oxidation occurs at the anode, so chlorine is evolved at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode, and the membrane also carries the current by passing ions.

electrochem-eng-008.question: In chlor-alkali electrolysis, which correctly describes a feature of the ion-exchange membrane process compared with the diaphragm and mercury processes?
choices: Mercury is used as the cathode to form sodium amalgam, which is reacted with water to obtain sodium hydroxide
Much salt remains in the catholyte, so the salt must be crystallized out and separated when the sodium hydroxide is concentrated
No mercury is used, and high-purity sodium hydroxide (about 30–35%) containing almost no sodium chloride is obtained directly from the cathode compartment
electrochem-eng-008.explanation: In the ion-exchange membrane process, the cation-exchange membrane prevents Cl⁻ from moving into the cathode compartment, so high-purity, low-salt sodium hydroxide is obtained directly at a concentration of about 30–35%. Because it uses no mercury and has a lower specific energy consumption, Japan shifted to it from the mercury and diaphragm processes, and it is now the main method. The option using mercury to form sodium amalgam describes the mercury process, which gives high purity but caused problems through mercury release into the environment. The option with much salt left in the catholyte is a feature of the diaphragm process: the porous diaphragm also passes brine, so the catholyte is NaOH of about 10% mixed with salt, and evaporative concentration is needed to separate the salt.

electrochem-eng-009.question: An ion-exchange membrane chlor-alkali cell is operated at a cell voltage of 3.0 V and a current efficiency of 95%. About how much electrical energy is needed to produce 1 t of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, molar mass 40.0 g/mol)? Take F = 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 1900 kWh
About 2100 kWh
About 4200 kWh
electrochem-eng-009.explanation: 1 t of NaOH is 1.0×10⁶ ÷ 40.0 = 2.50×10⁴ mol, and one electron flows for each OH⁻ formed at the cathode, so 1 mol of electrons is needed per mole of NaOH. With a current efficiency of 95%, the charge needed is Q = 2.50×10⁴ × 96485 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 2.54×10⁹ C, and the energy is 3.0 × 2.54×10⁹ ≈ 7.62×10⁹ J ≈ 2100 kWh. About 1900 kWh multiplies by the current efficiency instead of dividing by it, and about 4200 kWh applies the two electrons of the chlorine reaction 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ to 1 mol of NaOH. Raising the current density makes the plant smaller, but the cell voltage rises and the specific energy consumption gets worse.

electrochem-eng-010.question: Which correctly compares alkaline water electrolysis with polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) water electrolysis?
choices: PEM water electrolysis uses aqueous potassium hydroxide as the electrolyte, with OH⁻ moving through the membrane, so it can run on inexpensive nickel-based electrodes
In PEM electrolysis, H⁺ moves through a solid polymer membrane, allowing high current density on pure water, but precious-metal catalysts such as platinum and iridium oxide are required
In alkaline water electrolysis, H⁺ moves through the membrane in a strongly acidic environment, so acid-resistant precious-metal electrodes such as platinum and iridium oxide are essential
electrochem-eng-010.explanation: PEM water electrolysis uses a perfluorosulfonic acid cation-exchange membrane as the electrolyte; H⁺ produced at the anode passes through the membrane and becomes hydrogen at the cathode. The electrode gap is just the membrane thickness, so the resistance is low, and it suits high current densities of roughly 1–2 A/cm² or more and following fluctuating power, but the strongly acidic environment requires precious-metal catalysts such as platinum at the cathode and iridium oxide at the anode. Alkaline water electrolysis uses an aqueous KOH solution of about 25–30 wt% and a diaphragm, and OH⁻ moves through the electrolyte, so nickel-based electrodes can be used. The options in which PEM electrolysis uses aqueous KOH or in which H⁺ moves through a membrane in alkaline electrolysis mix up the features of the two.

electrochem-eng-011.question: In water electrolysis at 25 ℃, the theoretical decomposition voltage is 1.23 V and the thermoneutral voltage is 1.48 V. Which correctly describes the relationship between cell voltage and heat flow into or out of the cell?
choices: Once the cell voltage exceeds 1.23 V the electrical energy exceeds what decomposition needs, so the cell always generates heat at any voltage
Because the whole of ΔH must be supplied as electricity, electrolysis does not occur if the cell voltage is below 1.48 V
Between 1.23 V and 1.48 V the cell absorbs heat from outside, and above 1.48 V the surplus electrical energy is released as heat
electrochem-eng-011.explanation: The energy needed to split water is the enthalpy change ΔH (about 286 kJ/mol for liquid water at 25 ℃); of this, the Gibbs energy ΔG (about 237 kJ/mol) must be supplied as electricity, and the remainder TΔS can be supplied as heat. ΔG/(2F) is the theoretical decomposition voltage of 1.23 V, and ΔH/(2F) is the thermoneutral voltage of 1.48 V. When the cell voltage lies between them, electricity alone falls short of ΔH and the cell absorbs heat from its surroundings (and cools down unless heat is supplied); above 1.48 V the overpotential and ohmic loss become heat, so cooling is needed. Electrolysis can proceed above 1.23 V even below 1.48 V, so the option saying no electrolysis occurs below 1.48 V is wrong, and the option saying the cell always gives off heat overlooks the range in which the cell absorbs heat.

electrochem-eng-012.question: Copper is electrodeposited from a solution with a Cu²⁺ concentration of 100 mol/m³ (0.10 mol/L). Taking the diffusivity of Cu²⁺ as 7.0×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s and the thickness of the diffusion layer (film) at the electrode surface as 1.0×10⁻⁴ m, what is the limiting current density estimated from i_L = zFDC/δ? Take F = 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 135 A/m²
About 68 A/m²
About 0.14 A/m²
electrochem-eng-012.explanation: The limiting current is the current at which the Cu²⁺ concentration at the electrode surface falls to zero and the reaction rate is set solely by mass transfer through the diffusion layer. i_L = zFDC/δ = 2 × 96485 × 7.0×10⁻¹⁰ × 100 ÷ 1.0×10⁻⁴ ≈ 135 A/m². About 68 A/m² drops the electron number z = 2, and about 0.14 A/m² is a unit mistake from substituting the concentration as 0.10 in mol/L. The limiting current density is proportional to the mass transfer coefficient k = D/δ, so it increases when stirring or a higher liquid velocity thins the diffusion layer.

electrochem-eng-013.question: In electrodeposition, which correctly describes what happens when the current density approaches or exceeds the limiting current density?
choices: The metal ion concentration at the electrode surface rises so that the supply is ample, making dense, smooth deposits easier to obtain
The supply of metal ions cannot keep up, so deposits tend to become powdery or dendritic, and side reactions such as hydrogen evolution lower the current efficiency
The limiting current density is set by the electrode material alone and does not change with stirring, so exceeding it changes neither the deposit form nor the current efficiency
electrochem-eng-013.explanation: As the limiting current is approached, the metal ion concentration at the electrode surface approaches zero and the reaction becomes limited by supply through diffusion. Supply concentrates at the tips of protrusions, where it is locally favored, so deposits tend to become powdery or dendritic; raising the potential further does not increase the metal deposition current, and in aqueous solutions the current goes to side reactions such as hydrogen evolution, lowering the current efficiency. Industrial electrolysis is therefore run at current densities well below the limiting current density. The surface concentration falls rather than rises, so the option saying it rises is backwards. The limiting current density is inversely proportional to the diffusion layer thickness and increases with stirring, so the option saying stirring has no effect is also wrong.

electrochem-eng-014.question: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is operated at 25 ℃ with a cell voltage of 0.70 V. Taking the heat of combustion of hydrogen (higher heating value, HHV) as 286 kJ/mol and assuming all the hydrogen supplied reacts, what is the approximate electrical efficiency on an HHV basis? Take F = 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 83%
About 57%
About 47%
electrochem-eng-014.explanation: When 1 mol of hydrogen reacts, 2 mol of electrons flow, so the electrical energy obtained is 2FV = 2 × 96485 × 0.70 ≈ 1.35×10⁵ J = 135 kJ. Dividing by the HHV of hydrogen, 286 kJ, gives about 0.47, or about 47%, which is the same as 0.70 ÷ 1.48 (the thermoneutral voltage). About 83% is ΔG/ΔH = 237/286, the theoretical efficiency when the cell voltage equals the theoretical emf of 1.23 V. About 57% is the voltage efficiency 0.70 ÷ 1.23, not the electrical efficiency based on the heat of combustion. The more current drawn, the more the cell voltage falls because of overpotential and ohmic loss, and the lower the efficiency.

electrochem-eng-015.question: Which is correct about the charge–discharge energy efficiency of a secondary battery (energy taken out on discharge ÷ energy used for charging)?
choices: It is the product of the coulombic efficiency and the voltage efficiency (average discharge ÷ average charge voltage), and higher current raises overpotential and ohmic loss, lowering the voltage efficiency
If the coulombic efficiency is nearly 100%, the voltage losses on charge and discharge cancel out, so the energy efficiency is also nearly 100% regardless of the current
On discharge the overpotential and ohmic loss add to the emf, so the discharge voltage is always higher than the charge voltage and the voltage efficiency exceeds 1
electrochem-eng-015.explanation: The energy put in on charging is the charge passed × the average charge voltage, and the energy taken out is the discharge charge × the average discharge voltage, so energy efficiency = coulombic efficiency × voltage efficiency. For example, with a coulombic efficiency of 99%, an average charge voltage of 3.9 V and an average discharge voltage of 3.6 V, the result is 0.99 × 3.6/3.9 ≈ 0.91, or about 91%. On charging, overpotential and ohmic loss are added to the emf, and on discharging they are subtracted, so the discharge voltage is lower than the charge voltage, and the gap widens as the current increases. Even with a high coulombic efficiency the voltage losses remain, so the option claiming an energy efficiency of nearly 100% is wrong, and the option with a voltage efficiency above 1 has the voltages the wrong way round.
